item.title: Neuroscience of Asynchronous Development in the Bright Mind
item.description:
Child Development

Neuroscience of Asynchronous Development in the Bright Mind

Bright brains develop unevenly, requiring tailored support to thrive.

Posted August 7, 2026

Key points
  • Our individuality originates within our unique brains. Each is as distinctive as a fingerprint.
  • Children show asynchronous brain development, meaning regions of the brain grow at varying rates.
  • Regions that are developmentally behind compromise cognitive processing and executive functioning skills.
  • We need to pursue positive strategies and learning opportunities for each child.

“If you are always trying to be normal, you may never know how amazing you can be.”

--Maya Angelou

There is a great body of evidence in neuroscience indicating that our individuality originates within our unique brains.

Recent studies illuminate that each of our brains is as distinctive as a fingerprint. With advances in brain mapping and imaging software, we know no two brains are identical — which makes sense. We each have our own genetic makeup, process information from our environment through our five senses (sight, taste, touch, smell, and hearing) in our own ways, express unique ways of emotional processing, and have specific autobiographical memories. As a neuroscientist, I believe we are barely scratching the surface in our understanding of the human brain, both with regard to what we think we know and the vast world of the unknown. If you happen to be bright and have quirky behaviors, then your brain, body, and particular physiology may be at the core of how you navigate the world.

Early in 2006, a foundational study by Shaw and colleagues at the UCLA Imaging Institute followed more than 300 children for 12 years, mapping brain development and growth. They created three-dimensional brain maps and calculated measurements of grey and white matter from brain scans from ages seven to 19. In the study, the children completed an IQ test, and the participants were placed in three groups: average, high, and superior intelligence.

Researchers found that the children showed asynchronous brain development, meaning that regions of the brain grew at varying rates at various points in time. Brain growth was specific to the onset of puberty, when there is known to be vast brain expansions and major changes in the brain and body’s hormonal systems. Children in the superior intelligence group had an even greater increase in brain growth — specifically in the frontal cortex — from the onset of puberty through age 15.

The frontal cortex, which develops in humans all the way through the third decade of life, is the holy grail for executive functioning, intuitive problem-solving, communication, and emotional saliency. This is the mother lode for behavior and cognition, as well as planning, completing, and focusing on any sort of task. In bright children, a common challenge is remaining focused and being productive where there is a disconnect between their ability, functioning, and natural talents.

As we know, bright children often express extraordinary gifts but also have great challenges, which they either mask or are unaware of. Standard measures of intelligence, such as IQ tests, pose issues for 2e (twice exceptional) students because their weaknesses can preclude them from demonstrating their strengths. For instance, a child reading at a college level who struggles with writing may not be able to show the depth and complexity of her textual understanding; or my son, who was known as the absent-minded professor in middle school, did his work ahead of time but forgot to turn it in. Missing those assignments was not a true evaluation of his abilities or an understanding of his brainpower and functioning.

article continues after advertisement

Asynchronous brain development may be at the heart of what we are seeing in these bright children. There may be one or more greatly over-expanded and well-developed brain regions amidst other regions that are developmentally behind, compromising cognitive processing and executive functioning skills.

These are emerging perspectives about neurodiversity. To take a look at this more closely, imagine a three-year-old child with a well-developed brain area for audition (sensory processing for sound). For him, sounds are heard louder, sooner, and in some cases, the sounds can reach a threshold of pain for the child. Given the child’s age, an underdeveloped frontal cortex could make it difficult to regulate this threshold, resulting in bad behavior. A child could be tagged as a problem case rather than understood as having a specific disability that causes the child to suffer. This misidentification and misunderstanding could cause greater stress in the child and everyone around him, since the actual issue is not addressed.

Understanding that the frontal cortex greatly expands in puberty could be key to understanding asynchronous behavior in gifted and 2e children. When we see these troubling behaviors, it is critical that we completely understand their causes.

Are we doomed if we have a bright child? No, we simply have to pay closer attention to their particular ways of navigating the world. We need to pursue positive strategies and learning opportunities for the child. We know that learning requires an emotional connection to create positive associations and positive neural plasticity. The best ways to support a bright asynchronous learner are:

article continues after advertisement
  • Identify the origin of their learning difference
  • Implement appropriate accommodations
  • Allow them to learn at their own pace
  • Nurture strengths and challenges equally, providing more opportunities for success than failure.
  • Encourage divergent thinking
  • Find out what they love and let them run with it
  • Have them engage with like minds. This way they know they are not alone and become part of a community.

For my little absent-minded professor, a simple solution was creating a single homework folder that was turned in to his homeroom teacher at the start of the day. This gave him a foundation and a simple repetitive task, which then translated into positive behavior and feelings of success. Ultimately, we changed the mind-body connection with a positive solution. Also, this coincided with his natural development as his executive functioning skills caught up with his neurodiverse mind.

Mary Oliver wrote, “In creative work — creative work of all kinds — those who are the world’s working artists are not trying to help the world go around, but forward.”

It is our job as a society to find creative solutions to help these children thrive and move forward into a future where all shapes and sizes of neurodiversity are a way of life. As guides, we need to allow space and time for the bright mind to break free from the ordinary, experience the extraordinary, and then awaken to life.

item.title: Are You In a Wound Mate Relationship?
item.description:
Relationships

Are You In a Wound Mate Relationship?

Learn why you might be choosing painful romantic relationships.

Posted August 7, 2026

Key points
  • Wound mate relationships can mistake shared trauma for true intimacy and healthy connection.
  • Intense chemistry doesn't always signal love; it can reflect unresolved emotional wounds.
  • Repeatedly choosing similar wounded partners may come from confusing control with caring.

Having empathy for someone’s difficult past doesn’t mean you accept their current abusive behaviors.

In a wound mate relationship, you are locked into a defeating pattern where you bond with each other through your mutual wounds, trauma, and pain. This can feel intense and intimate, whether it’s a romance or any potentially close relationship. But actually, you may be confusing intensity with intimacy and control with caring.

You marvel at finding someone who is just like you and mistake them for a soulmate or soul friend. That’s why people who misuse substances are often attracted to each other and to other “wounded birds.” Or, yet again, you get involved with a narcissist who can manipulate your self-doubts and vulnerability, which draws you in.

In my book, The Genius of Empathy, I write about a patient who described her painful choices in romantic partners. She said, “I feel I have more in common with people who’ve had a diﬃcult childhood since I had one too. We ‘get’ each other.” With such seeming rapport, she was baﬄed about why the relationships failed. She didn’t understand that the same emotional wounds could prevent a partner from showing healthy intimacy. Nor did she grasp that the sizzling chemistry that can come from having a common history can’t always be equated with love. It often turns volatile and abusive with wound mates. So, in therapy, my patient started to accept that she was choosing wound mate relationships, which were unhealthy and painful. As she explored her own emotional patterns, such as needing to overgive to win someone’s love, she became attracted to potential partners who were more capable of intimacy.

If you identify with being a wound mate, you can begin to heal this pattern in psychotherapy, as my patient did. As a result of her emotional growth, she was able to become a caring partner who is more capable of intimacy. However, if you haven’t done this healing work, you could easily be drawn into these destructive relationships again, so be cautious.

The first step to healing this pattern is to be aware of it. Gently explore any beliefs that keep you repeating harmful relationships. Record them in a journal. Common ones are: “I only connect intimacy with pain,” or “A loving family yells at you because they care.” Tenderly replace these beliefs with more healing ones, such as: “Love means mutual respect,” or “Healthy intimacy feels comfortable and nurturing.” Have empathy for the beliefs that drew you to wound mates in the past so you can stay open to more emotionally available partners now.

To find a therapist, visit the Psychology Today Therapy Directory.

item.title: Identity: A Label or a Story?
item.description:
Identity

Identity: A Label or a Story?

Developing a robust narrative about our lives takes time.

Posted August 7, 2026

Key points
  • Identity experimentation and consolidation is an important part of adolescence and young adulthood.
  • A narrative identity is a personal story that reveals our values and offers a sense of continuity.
  • Young people are exposed to a wide array of possible identity labels online.
  • A label can be a starting point for wrestling with identity.
Source: Andrzej Gdula/Unsplash

When I arrived at college as a freshman in 1984, I met Chloe. She had long curly hair, trailed patchouli wherever she went, and seemed to have an endless selection of flowy, Indian print skirts. She listened to the Grateful Dead, fretted about getting tickets to their upcoming shows, and hung out with the kids playing hacky sack on the green during the warm, golden autumn we had that year. Chloe was a Dead Head.

Then I met someone who had gone to high school with Chloe. According to this person, a few short months before coming to college, Chloe owned no Indian print skirts and never smelled of patchouli. She didn’t listen to the Grateful Dead in any conspicuous way. Instead, she was a rather nondescript, somewhat nerdy kid whose socks sometimes didn’t match. It seemed clear what had happened. Given the opportunity for a fresh start in a new place, Chloe had adopted a new identity, one that came with a fully formed set of tastes and behaviors and offered a sense of belonging.

The American psychoanalyst Erik Erickson was one of the first to discuss explicitly the importance of identity exploration and consolidation in adolescence. According to Erikson, identity has two main functions, one intrapsychic, and one interpersonal – it helps create a coherent sense of self, and it connects us with a group with whom we share an essential characteristic. In other words, one’s personal identity answers the question “who am I?” and “how do I fit into the world around me?” Jung noted that, with the declining influence of the dominant cultural stories offered by religions and with increasing cultural fragmentation, the task of creating a stable identity from which one can negotiate the world becomes a task for each individual, often at the cusp of adulthood.

American psychologist Dan McAdams has pointed out that a full identity is a story – a narrative identity. The stories we tell ourselves provide us with a sense of continuity, identity, and meaning. A narrative identity is a kind of personal myth that elucidates key values. “The personal myth…” writes McAdams, “is a sacred story that embodies personal truth.”1 This personal myth-making largely happens unconsciously, but as the story of Chloe illustrates, there are times when we consciously adopt an identity for ourselves.

In our atomized, demythologized modern world, the work of identity consolidation is more confusing than it used to be, and demands more of us individually. Without collectively sanctioned grand narratives to offer us central organizing values, we must each choose from a chaotic welter of available stories to make sense of our lives. Chloe adopted an identity that was readily available in the collective in 1984. The knowledge of what a Dead Head was and how to be one was widely disseminated. Once Chloe picked that for herself, she had a script to follow.

Today, young people are finding a plethora of identity labels online. Whether they choose to define themselves according to typology (Introvert/extrovert), lifestyle and aesthetics (Goblincore, Goth, etc.), or even according to fictional types (Trekkie, Ravenclaw, Jedi), the internet is replete with a rich vocabulary of potential identity labels.

Labels can offer us structure while we explore who we are and what matters to us. Through them, we can find meaning, solidarity, and belonging with like-minded others. However, adopting a label should be the beginning of identity exploration, not the end. Labels differ from narrative identity in a fundamental way. McAdams stresses that the development of a personal narrative is effortful, hard-won, and individual. According to McAdams, a personal myth “evolves slowly over time.”2 In contrast, identities on offer online tend to be ready-made and algorithmically suggested.

A label is reductive and general, while a story that has been wrestled into being through repeated efforts is dynamic, layered, and wholly personal. A label can be a starting point in one’s search for a sustaining personal myth, but if we don’t find a way to live the identity and make it fully our own, it can become limiting and constricting. What does it mean to be a be a certain type of person in the different areas of our lives? Does our identity help us to navigate difficult decisions or moments of crisis? How does an identity serve us – or not – in the realm of our most intimate relationships? There is always a risk that if we cling too tightly to a rigid identity, we will find our sense of self impoverished and foreclosed. This can happen when a label is used not just for self-understanding and solidarity, but as a means of escaping unpleasant developmental milestones or retreating from life and relationships.

Chloe continued to love the Grateful Dead’s music and dress the part. However, over the course of our first year, I noticed a subtle change in her. She got excited by her neuroscience classes and spent more time talking about those than ostentatiously scheming about how to get Dead tickets. She gradually seemed a bit more relaxed and put less effort into making sure everyone knew she was a Dead Head. She even wore less patchouli. Though she and I didn’t stay in touch past our freshman year, I imagine that her newly adopted identity helped her adjust to college, find a ready-made friend group, and access a scaffold from which she could grow. But it didn’t ultimately define or limit her.

item.title: I'm Not a President, but I Play One on TV
item.description:
Politics

I'm Not a President, but I Play One on TV

Celebrity, evolution, bias, and politics in the modern age.

Posted August 7, 2026

Key points
  • Going back to the Reagan presidency, US voters have supported various celebrities for elected positions.
  • While celebrities may have what it takes to succeed in elected office, they may not as well.
  • Based on an evolutionary perspective, it is noteworthy that celebrity was not a thing for most of our history.
  • The tendency to think that celebrities' public images can replace actual expertise is highly concerning.
Source: Aaron Kittredge / Pexels

Here are some celebrities who have emerged as elected leaders in the United States:

  • Ronald Reagan, actor—Governor of California and President of the United States
  • Jesse the Body Ventura, professional wrestler—Governor of Minnesota
  • Arnold Schwarzenegger, body builder and actor—Governor of California
  • Al Franken, actor/comedian—US Senator representing Minnesota

  • Donald Trump, reality TV star/business person—President of the United States

    Aside from the quizzical fact that Minnesota and California—wildly different states from each other—seem particularly prone toward electing officials who have backgrounds in the field of entertainment (now there's a research question for you!), the fact that several officials in some of the highest offices in the nation have backgrounds in the entertainment industry should give anyone pause.

    Running a Government Is Not Something That Just Anyone Can Do

    While government and political science are not my field of expertise, like many of us, I took a course or two on government and history back in the day. I remember an AP US History course with Mr. Raby in about 1987. This course was no joke. The details of the three branches of government, the nuts and bolts of the US Constitution, the historical reasons for things like the electoral college, historical relations between the US and other nations around the world, etc., were not exactly common knowledge—not by a long shot.

    There is a reason that people who work in specialized fields have educational and work-related backgrounds in those fields. I don't want my airplane pilot to have the experience of having played a pilot in the movies. I don't want the person building my house to be someone who played a contractor on a TV show. And I don't want my surgeon to be someone who got the job simply by having played a surgeon on TV.

    To think that educational background and expertise are not relevant for taking on a position as an elected official is simply naive. So why do so many of us seem to think that actors with no background in government are suitable for some of the highest elected positions in the nation?

    Why Do We Think That Celebrities Match the Characters That They Play?

    Two critical psychological concepts that shed light on this issue include evolutionary mismatch (see Geher & Wedberg, 2022) and dispositionist bias (see Ross & Nisbett, 1991). Evolutionary mismatch, broadly, refers to situations in which an organism's current environment is mismatched from the ancestral environments that surrounded that organism's evolutionary history. For most of human evolution, actors on TV shows were not a thing. So our minds evolved to make inferences about people's characteristics based on behaviors that they displayed—and doing so was usually a good bet as to what that person was like in an overall sense. This same process, inferring people's traits based on their behaviors, doesn't work that well when we are talking about celebrities from the entertainment industry.

    For instance, Jesse the Body Ventura played a wild, beast of a man in his wrestling persona—truly a character. A character that only somewhat reflected who he was when not in-character. The same is true, in varying degrees, with all celebrities who portray a specific character when on-stage or in front of the camera. Without commenting on his job as governor, it is noteworthy that Ventura (actually, James George Janos), never obtained a college degree (although he did have substantial military experience). When you think about it, it's hard to wrap one's mind around how someone who does not have expert-level understanding of economics, state government, levels of government and how they interface with one another, electoral processes, healthcare policy, educational policy, relevant historical knowledge, etc., is qualified to serve as the primary executive of an entire state. This is not a slight on the former Minnesota governor—it is simply an observation.

    When he was running for office, he clearly came across as strong, charismatic, funny, and likeable. All these traits can, in fact, trace back to the fact that his primary work experience was as a professional wrestler. That said, humans are so inclined to believe that people's internal traits match their observable behavior that he was able to get himself elected into an extremely high position. Our minds are not evolved to discriminate between one's celebrity persona from one's actual core personality traits and knowledge base. The fact that celebrity is even a thing in the modern era is a clear example of evolutionary mismatch in the modern human experience.

    Related, people in individualistic cultures such as the United States often tend to lean toward what is known as the dispositionist bias. This bias basically is a tendency to think that people's actions are caused by factors inside themselves. Such internal characteristics include enduring personality traits, emotional states, and attitudes—among others. When we see someone express angry behavior, we infer that this person may well be nasty and have anger issues. When we see someone do something helpful for someone else, we infer that this person has a kind disposition that likely cuts across various situations.

    So when minds that are colored by the dispositionist bias see the movie The Terminator, we tend to think that the actor (in this case Arnold Schwarzenegger) has all the characteristics of the character that he is playing. We may think that he is strong, powerful, capable, etc. This is the magic of Hollywood. And without commenting on Arnold's work as governor, it stands to reason that backgrounds in weightlifting and acting are not exactly standard requisites for understanding the many complexities of the governmental structure, natural history, and cultural history of the Golden State.

    Bottom Line

    Wherever you are on the political spectrum, you likely agree that the world is a mess right now. And a large part of this problem stems from politics at the international and national levels (among others).

    The US, home to Hollywood and so many other hubs of the international entertainment industry, has a long history of having elected officials whose backgrounds are found in that industry as opposed to government, economics, history, policy, or politics—fields that actually relate to serving as an elected government official.

    I would argue that this trend, which seems to be rooted in both evolutionary mismatch and the dispositionist bias, is at least somewhat problematic. I don't want my surgeon's primary qualification to be that they played one on TV. And I don't want my elected official's primary qualification to be that they were a champion body builder.

    Given how much is on the line in the current political landscape—at all levels—it may behoove us to cultivate a culture of caution regarding celebrity candidates for elected positions. This is not to say that a celebrity is sure to fail as an elected official. But at the very least, perhaps voters should consider the relevance of their experience when going to the polls.

    After all, the world that we will leave to future generations is on the line.
